subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Coffeehouses in Mecca and Cairo
description: A fast breakdown of Coffeehouses in Mecca and Cairo for builders.

hook.text: Before Constantinople, coffee was already being served publicly in Mecca and Cairo as early as the 1500s.

buildup.text: Sufi monks used coffee to stay awake for nighttime prayers. Communal brewing spread to lay gatherings.

discovery.text: Cairo's coffeehouses became hubs for Sufi poetry recitals, storytelling, and philosophical exchange.

twist.text: Religious authorities in Mecca banned coffee in 1511, calling it an intoxicant. The ban lasted only 13 years.

climax.text: The Ottoman governor of Egypt overturned the ban. Coffee was too popular and too profitable to suppress.

punchline.text: Even Mecca couldn't ban coffee. The drink was already unstoppable.

quiz.question: Why did religious authorities in Mecca ban coffee in 1511?

details.summary: Coffee drinking began as a Sufi practice in Yemen before spreading to coffeehouses in Mecca and Cairo in the early 1500s. These establishments served as gathering places for scholars, merchants, and travelers.
details.whyItMatters: Mecca and Cairo were where coffee transitioned from a religious aid to a commercial and social beverage. Their coffeehouses set the pattern for global adoption.
takeaways: Coffeehouses in Mecca and Cairo date to the early 1500s
They served scholars, merchants, and Sufi practitioners

faq.question: Why was coffee controversial in the Islamic world?
faq.answer: Some scholars argued that coffee was an intoxicant forbidden under Islamic dietary law. Others pointed out it was not explicitly mentioned in the Quran and that it aided prayer and study. The debate raged for decades, but coffee's popularity ultimately overcame opposition.

faq.question: How did Sufi mystics use coffee?
faq.answer: Sufis used coffee to stay awake during long nighttime prayer sessions and dhikr ceremonies. They recognized its stimulant properties and valued it as a spiritual aid. This religious use gave coffee early legitimacy before it became a secular social drink.
